items.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease has a serum potassium that has risen from 5.0 mmol/L to 6.8 mmol/L (5.0 to 6.8 mEq/L) over 2 days. Which change on the cardiac monitor is typically the EARLIEST ECG sign of this electrolyte imbalance?

options.text: Prominent U waves following flattened T waves
Tall, narrow, peaked T waves
A prolonged QT interval
A sine-wave pattern

rationales.A: Incorrect. Flattened or depressed T waves with prominent U waves are the ECG pattern of hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.
rationales.B: Correct. As potassium rises, tall, symmetric, peaked T waves are usually the first visible ECG change; with further increases the PR interval lengthens, the P wave disappears and the QRS widens.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hyperkalemia tends to shorten, not lengthen, the QT interval. A prolonged QT interval is characteristic of severe hypocalcemia.
rationales.D: Incorrect. A sine-wave pattern is a late, pre-arrest finding that appears after QRS widening, just before ventricular fibrillation or asystole; it is not the earliest sign.

items.topic: Hyperkalemia — ECG progression
items.units_note: Potassium in mmol/L is numerically equal to mEq/L.

sources.evidence: ECG changes often visible when K > 5.5 mmol/L; tall, symmetric, peaked T waves initially; >6.5 mmol/L widened QRS, loss of P wave; finally sine wave then VF/asystole; QT shortening.

items.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes who uses insulin reports feeling shaky and sweaty 2 hours before lunch. The client is alert and able to swallow. Capillary blood glucose is 3.1 mmol/L (56 mg/dL). For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated at this time.

rows.text: Give 15 g of carbohydrate as glucose tablets.
Recheck the capillary blood glucose 15 minutes after treatment.
Give a second 15 g of carbohydrate immediately, before any recheck, to prevent recurrence.
After the hypoglycemia resolves, offer a snack containing carbohydrate and protein because lunch is more than 1 hour away.

rationales.R1: Indicated. Mild-to-moderate hypoglycemia in a conscious adult is treated with 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate; Diabetes Canada prefers glucose or sucrose tablets or solution.
rationales.R2: Indicated. Blood glucose is retested about 15 minutes after treatment, and another 15 g is given only if it is still low (Diabetes Canada: below 4.0 mmol/L).
rationales.R3: Not indicated. Glucagon 1 mg SC/IM is reserved for severe hypoglycemia when the person cannot take oral carbohydrate (for example, is unconscious) and IV access is not available. This client is alert and can swallow.
rationales.R4: Not indicated. Re-treatment depends on the 15-minute recheck. Giving extra carbohydrate without rechecking risks overtreatment, which can cause rebound hyperglycemia and weight gain.
rationales.R5: Indicated. Once hypoglycemia is reversed, a snack with about 15 g of carbohydrate plus a protein source is recommended when the next meal is more than 1 hour away, to prevent recurrence.

items.topic: Hypoglycemia management in a conscious adult (rule of 15)
items.jurisdiction_note: Diabetes Canada defines hypoglycemia (insulin/secretagogue users) as plasma glucose <4.0 mmol/L and re-treats if still <4.0; Merck (US) uses <3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) and re-treats if not >4.4 mmol/L (80 mg/dL). The stem value (3.1 mmol/L) is low under both, and the threshold difference is not tested.

items.stem: In an Ontario hospital, a 79-year-old client has been found incapable with respect to a proposed surgical treatment. The client's spouse, adult son, and sister are at the bedside. The chart contains a valid power of attorney for personal care that appoints the client's niece and gives her authority over treatment decisions. The niece is capable, available, and willing to act. Under Ontario law, who is the appropriate substitute decision-maker to give or refuse consent for this treatment?

options.text: The client's spouse
The client's niece
The client's adult son
The Public Guardian and Trustee

rationales.A: Incorrect. Under the Health Care Consent Act, 1996, a spouse or partner ranks below an attorney for personal care whose power of attorney covers treatment decisions.
rationales.B: Correct. An attorney for personal care with authority over treatment ranks above a spouse, children and siblings in the Act's list of substitute decision-makers. Because the niece is capable, available and willing, consent is obtained from her as the highest-ranked substitute decision-maker.
rationales.C: Incorrect. A child of the incapable person ranks below both the attorney for personal care and the spouse.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Public Guardian and Trustee decides only as a last resort, when no one on the list meets the requirements to act. A qualified attorney for personal care is available here.

items.jurisdiction_note: Ranking set by Ontario's Health Care Consent Act, 1996, s. 20 (guardian; attorney for personal care; Board-appointed representative; spouse/partner; child or parent; parent with access only; sibling; other relative; PGT as last resort). Other provinces and US states use different surrogate laws; NCLEX items generally use generic advance-directive/health care proxy wording.

items.stem: A client admitted to a medical unit has had a productive cough for 3 weeks with night sweats and weight loss, and active pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected. Which measures should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place the client in an airborne infection isolation room with negative air flow.
Wear a fit-tested, seal-checked N95 respirator when entering the room.
Keep the room door closed whether or not the client is in the room.
Have the client wear a mask if transport out of the room is necessary.
Wear a surgical mask instead of a respirator, because tuberculosis spreads by large droplets.
Allow staff who report a previous tuberculosis infection to enter without a respirator.

rationales.A: Correct. Suspected or confirmed pulmonary or laryngeal TB requires Airborne Precautions in a single airborne infection isolation room with negative air flow.
rationales.B: Correct. Staff entering the room of a client with suspected active pulmonary TB must wear a fit-tested, seal-checked N95 (or higher) respirator.
rationales.C: Correct. The door of an airborne isolation room must stay closed to keep the negative-pressure air flow working; Ontario's PIDAC guidance says it is kept closed whether or not the client is in the room.
rationales.D: Correct. Transport out of the room is limited to what is necessary, and the client wears a mask during transport (if tolerated) for source control.
rationales.E: Incorrect. TB spreads by the airborne route in small droplet nuclei that stay suspended in air. A surgical mask does not reliably protect the wearer from inhaling them; an N95 respirator is the minimum.
rationales.F: Incorrect. The N95 requirement for active pulmonary TB applies to all staff. Immunity-based exceptions in Ontario's precautions apply to diseases such as measles and varicella, not TB.

items.stem: A client with heart failure and peripheral edema has an order for furosemide 40 mg IV now. The vial is labelled furosemide injection 10 mg/mL. How many millilitres should the nurse prepare? Round to the nearest whole number.

rationales.calculation: Volume = dose ordered ÷ concentration = 40 mg ÷ 10 mg/mL = 4 mL. Check: 4 mL × 10 mg/mL = 40 mg. The dose is within the usual initial adult IV dose for edema in the Canadian product monograph and US labelling (20 to 40 mg as a single dose), and IV furosemide is given slowly over 1 to 2 minutes.

items.stem: After removing gloves following a routine bed bath, a nurse's hands are not visibly soiled. According to Ontario PIDAC hand-hygiene guidance (concordant with CDC clinical safety guidance), which action is preferred?

options.text: Wash with soap and running water for at least 2 minutes.
Apply a 70–90% alcohol-based hand rub and rub until dry.
Rinse briefly with water only; no product is needed after glove removal.
Apply a non-alcohol waterless antiseptic foam as first choice.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Soap and water is required when hands are visibly soiled (or in certain spore-related situations). When hands are not visibly soiled, alcohol-based hand rub is preferred.
rationales.B: Correct. When hands are not visibly soiled, a 70–90% alcohol-based hand rub is the preferred method in Ontario health-care settings and is also preferred by CDC in most clinical situations.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hand hygiene is still required after glove removal; rinsing with water alone is not an accepted method.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Non-alcohol-based waterless antiseptic agents are not recommended for hand hygiene in health-care settings.

items.stem: A nurse finishes care for a client with laboratory-confirmed Clostridioides difficile infection, removes gloves and gown, and finds a dedicated hand-washing sink immediately available. Hands are not visibly soiled. Which hand-hygiene method is preferred in this situation?

options.text: Apply alcohol-based hand rub only, because hands are not visibly soiled.
Wash with soap and water at the dedicated sink.
Wash with soap and water at the client's bathroom sink for convenience.
Skip hand hygiene because Contact Precautions gloves already protected the hands.

rationales.A: Incorrect. For C. difficile, soap and water is theoretically more effective at removing spores than alcohol-based hand rub when a dedicated sink is available.
rationales.B: Correct. PIDAC advises that when C. difficile is diagnosed or suspected and a dedicated hand-washing sink is immediately available, hands should be washed with soap and water. CDC likewise recommends soap and water during care of clients with C. difficile in outbreak settings.
rationales.C: Incorrect. PIDAC specifically advises not to perform hand hygiene at the client's sink because that may re-contaminate the health-care provider's hands.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Meticulous hand hygiene is required after glove removal; gloves do not replace hand hygiene.

items.stem: During a skin assessment, the nurse finds intact skin over a client's sacral bony prominence with a localized area of nonblanchable erythema. Sensation over the area is slightly increased compared with surrounding skin. How should this finding be documented?

options.text: Stage 1 pressure injury
Stage 2 pressure injury
Unstageable pressure injury
Deep-tissue pressure injury

rationales.A: Correct. Stage 1 is intact skin with localized nonblanchable erythema, often over a bony prominence; changes in sensation, temperature, or firmness may accompany it.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Stage 2 involves partial-thickness skin loss (shallow open ulcer or blister) with a pink/red wound bed, not intact skin alone.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Unstageable injuries have full-thickness loss obscured by slough or eschar so depth cannot be determined.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Deep-tissue pressure injury presents as persistent nonblanchable deep red, maroon, or purple discoloration, not simple nonblanchable erythema of Stage 1.

items.stem: A client is confined to bed after major abdominal surgery and is assessed as high risk for pressure injury. Which repositioning schedule best reflects evidence-based pressure-reduction practice?

options.text: Turn the client at least every 2 hours using a written schedule.
Turn the client once every 8-hour shift if the skin remains intact.
Keep the client supine continuously for the first 24 postoperative hours.
Reposition only when the client requests a position change.

rationales.A: Correct. Frequent repositioning is the most important pressure-reduction factor; bed-confined clients should be turned at least every 2 hours with a written schedule to direct and document the turns.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Waiting until every 8 hours is far less frequent than the minimum every-2-hour turning recommended for bed-confined clients.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Continuous supine positioning increases pressure-injury risk; early and scheduled repositioning is needed.
rationales.D: Incorrect. High-risk clients need a scheduled repositioning plan; relying only on client request is insufficient.

items.stem: An adult with type 1 diabetes is admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis. Intravenous 0.9% saline has been started. The first serum potassium result is 3.0 mmol/L (3.0 mEq/L). Which action regarding insulin therapy is appropriate at this time?

options.text: Begin regular insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h IV immediately to correct the acidosis.
Withhold insulin temporarily, replace potassium, and start insulin once potassium is at least 3.3 mmol/L.
Give subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin only; intravenous insulin is not used in adult DKA.
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate first; insulin is unnecessary if bicarbonate is corrected.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Starting insulin while potassium is below 3.3 mmol/L risks dangerous further hypokalemia because insulin drives potassium into cells.
rationales.B: Correct. If serum potassium is below 3.3 mmol/L, insulin is withheld (or stopped) while potassium is replaced until potassium is at least 3.3 mmol/L. Diabetes Canada also emphasizes fluid resuscitation, avoidance of hypokalemia, and insulin as core DKA principles.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Adult DKA requires intravenous insulin (Diabetes Canada: 0.1 units/kg/h) for resolution; subcutaneous-only regimens are not the standard emergency approach described here.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Bicarbonate is considered only for extreme acidosis (pH ≤7.0) and does not replace insulin therapy.

items.stem: A client with heart failure takes digoxin daily and was recently started on furosemide. Which laboratory finding most increases the risk of digoxin toxicity?

options.text: Serum potassium 2.9 mmol/L (2.9 mEq/L)
Serum sodium 138 mmol/L (138 mEq/L)
Hemoglobin 128 g/L (12.8 g/dL)
Serum glucose 5.8 mmol/L (104 mg/dL)

rationales.A: Correct. Hypokalemia sensitizes the myocardium to digoxin so toxicity may occur even when the digoxin level is in the usual range. Potassium-depleting diuretics such as furosemide increase this risk.
rationales.B: Incorrect. A sodium of 138 mmol/L is within a typical reference interval and is not the classic precipitant of digoxin toxicity highlighted in labelling.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hemoglobin near 128 g/L does not specifically increase digoxin toxicity risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. A glucose of 5.8 mmol/L is not a recognized precipitant of digoxin toxicity in the cited sources.

items.stem: Before giving the morning digoxin tablet, the nurse counts the client's apical pulse for 1 full minute and obtains 52 beats/min. The client is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.text: Administer the digoxin as scheduled because the client has no symptoms.
Withhold the digoxin and notify the health-care provider.
Give half the ordered dose and recheck the pulse in 30 minutes.
Crush the tablet and give it with a high-potassium food to prevent toxicity.

rationales.A: Incorrect. An apical rate under 60 beats/min is an indication to withhold digoxin pending provider guidance, even if the client currently feels well.
rationales.B: Correct. Nursing practice guidance is to assess the pulse for 1 minute and not administer digoxin if the heart rate is less than 60 beats/min. The Canadian monograph likewise notes that bradycardia related to digoxin may require temporary withdrawal and monitoring.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Nurses do not independently halve digoxin doses; the dose should be withheld and the provider notified.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Crushing is not indicated solely for a low pulse, and giving the dose despite bradycardia is unsafe.

items.stem: A client with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation is started on warfarin for stroke prevention. The nurse reinforces teaching about the usual therapeutic INR target range for this indication. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding?

options.text: My INR goal is usually about 2.0 to 3.0.
My INR should stay below 1.0 at all times.
An INR above 5.0 is ideal for preventing clots.
Warfarin does not require blood-test monitoring once I feel well.

rationales.D: Incorrect. Warfarin dosing is adjusted according to PT/INR results and requires ongoing monitoring.

items.stem: A client arrives in the emergency department with sudden unilateral arm weakness and slurred speech that began 2 hours ago. Non-contrast CT has excluded intracranial hemorrhage, and a physician with stroke expertise confirms eligibility for intravenous thrombolysis. Within what time from symptom onset (or last known well) should intravenous alteplase or tenecteplase ideally be started for standard-window treatment?

options.text: Within 4.5 hours
Within 24 hours only; earlier treatment is not beneficial
Within 72 hours after a completed stroke work-up
Only if symptoms have been present for at least 12 hours

rationales.A: Correct. Canadian Stroke Best Practices recommend offering IV thrombolysis with alteplase or tenecteplase to eligible patients who can be treated within 4.5 hours of onset or last known well. OpenStax likewise states thrombolytics must be given within about 3–4.5 hours of onset.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Waiting up to 24 hours as the only window is incorrect for standard IV thrombolysis; benefit is highly time-dependent within the early window (extended imaging-selected windows are a separate pathway).
rationales.C: Incorrect. A 72-hour delay is far outside the standard IV thrombolysis window.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Treatment should be as soon as possible after arrival; requiring 12 hours of symptoms would miss the therapeutic window.

items.stem: Fifteen minutes after starting a packed red blood cell transfusion, a client reports chills and new flank pain. Temperature has risen from 36.8°C to 38.2°C. After the nurse stops the transfusion, which concurrent action is most appropriate?

options.text: Flush the blood tubing with the remaining packed cells to clear the line.
Keep the intravenous line open with normal saline using new tubing, and notify the blood bank.
Restart the same unit at a slower rate after giving acetaminophen.
Discard the blood bag immediately so it cannot be returned for investigation.

items.stem: A postoperative client has brisk wound drainage into a surgical drain. The client is anxious. Capillary refill is delayed, skin is cool and clammy, heart rate is 118 beats/min, and blood pressure is 118/78 mm Hg. Which interpretation best fits these findings?

options.text: Early compensatory response to hypovolemia; tachycardia can precede frank hypotension.
Cardiogenic shock is most likely because blood pressure is still near the client's baseline.
Findings are reassuring; hypovolemic shock is excluded until systolic blood pressure falls below 90 mm Hg.
Neurogenic shock is most likely because the client is anxious after surgery.

rationales.A: Correct. In early hypovolemic compensation, sympathetic activation raises heart rate and vascular tone; blood pressure may remain normal or only slightly changed while tachycardia, cool clammy skin, and anxiety appear.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Cardiogenic shock involves pump failure; this picture of volume loss with compensatory tachycardia fits hypovolemia, not a primary cardiac pump problem.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hypotension is common in shock but is not required early; clients may be normotensive while compensation is still effective.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Neurogenic shock typically features bradycardia and warm dry skin from loss of sympathetic tone, not compensatory tachycardia with cool clammy skin.

items.stem: Immediately after a term vaginal birth, the vigorous newborn is placed on the birthing person's chest. Which nursing action best prevents evaporative heat loss in the first minutes of life?

options.text: Delay drying until the first bath so vernix can protect the skin.
Dry the newborn thoroughly and then keep the infant covered or in skin-to-skin contact.
Place the wet newborn under a fan to promote convective cooling.
Leave the newborn uncovered on a cool scale for an immediate accurate weight.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Amniotic fluid on the skin causes evaporative heat loss; drying should not be delayed for that reason in the delivery setting.
rationales.B: Correct. Evaporative heat loss occurs as wet amniotic fluid vaporizes; immediate drying followed by covering or skin-to-skin contact is a primary prevention step for neonatal hypothermia.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Forced cool airflow increases convective heat loss and is opposite of thermal protection.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Contact with a cool surface and prolonged exposure promote conductive and radiant heat loss.

items.stem: A postpartum client has Rh-negative blood and is not already sensitized. The newborn's blood type is Rh-positive. Which action is indicated?

options.text: Administer Rho(D) immune globulin within 72 hours of birth.
Withhold Rho(D) immune globulin because sensitization only occurs in subsequent pregnancies and never after the first birth.
Give Rho(D) immune globulin only if the client's direct Coombs test is already positive.
Delay Rho(D) immune globulin until the 6-week postpartum visit so antibodies can form first.

rationales.A: Correct. An unsensitized Rh-negative parent who delivers an Rh-positive newborn should receive Rho(D) immune globulin, typically within 72 hours, to prevent alloimmunization that could harm future pregnancies.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Fetomaternal hemorrhage at birth can sensitize the parent after the current pregnancy; postpartum prophylaxis exists to prevent that sensitization.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Prophylaxis is for clients who are not already sensitized; a positive antibody screen indicating sensitization changes management and is not the indication for routine Rho(D) immune globulin.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Waiting weeks allows time for sensitization; the standard window is within 72 hours after birth.

items.stem: A client with alcohol use disorder is beginning medically supervised withdrawal. Which interventions are appropriate components of withdrawal care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Administer prescribed benzodiazepines based on withdrawal severity.
Give thiamine to help prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
Start routine daily phenytoin for every client even without a seizure disorder.
Use haloperidol alone as the first medication for autonomic hyperactivity.
Continue high-dose benzodiazepines indefinitely after detoxification for craving control.

rationales.A: Correct. Benzodiazepines are the mainstay for alcohol-withdrawal agitation and seizure prevention.
rationales.B: Correct. Thiamine is given during withdrawal care to help prevent Wernicke encephalopathy associated with thiamine deficiency.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Routine phenytoin is not indicated for uncomplicated alcohol-withdrawal seizures.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Antipsychotics are not recommended as initial monotherapy and may lower the seizure threshold.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Benzodiazepines used for detoxification should not continue after the detoxification period.

items.stem: An 78-year-old hospitalized client develops sudden confusion that worsens at night, has difficulty focusing attention, and returns nearly to baseline later the same day. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: Findings are typical of Alzheimer dementia because cognition declined overnight.
Findings suggest delirium: an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition that warrants evaluation for a medical cause.
Fluctuating attention excludes delirium and confirms a primary psychotic disorder.
No further assessment is needed once orientation returns briefly to baseline.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Dementia typically has a more gradual course and primarily affects memory; an abrupt, fluctuating inattention pattern is characteristic of delirium, which can occur in people with or without underlying dementia.
rationales.B: Correct. Delirium is an acute, usually reversible, fluctuating disturbance in attention, cognition, and consciousness that often signals an underlying medical problem and requires prompt evaluation.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Fluctuating attention is a hallmark of delirium, not a finding that excludes it.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Temporary clearing does not remove the need to identify and treat the precipitating cause.

items.stem: A client is admitted with suspected seasonal influenza and is placed on Droplet Precautions in a private room. Which personal protective equipment action is required when the nurse enters the room for routine care?

options.text: Don a fit-tested N95 respirator and keep the door closed at all times as for airborne isolation.
Don a facemask upon room entry and remove it after leaving the room, with hand hygiene.
Enter without a mask if standing more than one metre from the client.
Wear sterile gloves and a sterile gown for every entry, even without anticipated contact with body fluids.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Seasonal influenza is managed with Droplet Precautions; an N95 and airborne (negative-pressure) setup are not the routine requirement for standard droplet care.
rationales.B: Correct. For Droplet Precautions, including suspected or confirmed influenza, health-care personnel don a facemask on room entry and remove/dispose of it on exit with hand hygiene.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Guidance directs masking upon entry into the droplet precaution space, not only during close contact at an arbitrary distance.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Sterile gown and sterile gloves are not the droplet PPE standard for routine entry; gown/gloves follow Standard Precautions when contact with body fluids is anticipated.

items.stem: A nurse in Ontario finishes documenting for an assigned client. A colleague asks the nurse to look up laboratory results in the electronic record of a neighbour who is not on the nurse's assignment and for whom the nurse has no care role. Which response best meets confidentiality and privacy accountabilities?

options.text: Access the neighbour's chart briefly because curiosity among staff is an accepted professional purpose.
Decline to access the record, explaining that personal health information may be accessed only when needed for an authorized care purpose.
Print the full chart and leave it at the nursing station so anyone on the unit can answer questions.
Share the neighbour's results aloud in the cafeteria so the colleague does not need system access.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Accessing a record without a professional care purpose violates CNO confidentiality standards and PHIPA limits on collection and use.
rationales.B: Correct. Nurses must access only the personal health information needed for an authorized purpose; PHIPA requires that no more personal health information be collected, used, or disclosed than is reasonably necessary.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Leaving identifiable charts available for unnecessary viewing increases unauthorized access risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Discussing client information in public places such as cafeterias breaches confidentiality.

items.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has severe neutropenia. The client reports feeling unwell. Oral temperature is 38.5°C. There is no obvious focus of infection on brief examination. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Document the temperature and reassess in 4 hours before notifying the provider.
Recognize fever as a presumed serious infection and promptly notify the provider so empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics can be started.
Encourage fresh fruit and a floral arrangement to improve nutrition and mood while awaiting culture results.
Hold all antimicrobial therapy until a definitive organism is identified on culture.

rationales.A: Incorrect. In severe neutropenia, fever is treated as a medical emergency; waiting hours delays needed empiric therapy.
rationales.B: Correct. When severe neutropenia is present, fever usually indicates infection even if a focus is not obvious, and immediate empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics are required.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Neutropenic precautions include avoiding fresh fruit and fresh flowers because of infection risk; these are not supportive measures during febrile neutropenia.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Empiric antibiotics are started promptly; waiting for culture identification is unsafe in febrile neutropenia.
